# 1. Correlation

## Is a Richer Country a Healthier One?

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.6))
ax.scatter(g2007["gdpPercap"], g2007["lifeExp"])
ax.set(xlabel="GDP per capita (dollars)", ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
plt.show()
```

- In 2007, countries with higher incomes tend to have longer lives
- **Correlation** sums this up in one number

## Correlation

```{python}
print(round(g2007["gdpPercap"].corr(g2007["lifeExp"]), 2))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(1118)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9, 1.5))
for ax, r in zip(axes, [-0.8, 0, 0.5, 0.95]):
    x = rng.normal(size=150)
    y = r * x + np.sqrt(1 - r ** 2) * rng.normal(size=150)
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=6)
    ax.set_title(f"r = {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]:.2f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- `r` runs from −1 to +1 and measures how close the points are to **a straight line**
- Its sign gives the **direction**, its size the **strength**. Here, 0.68: up together

## Several Columns at Once

```{python}
g2007[["lifeExp", "gdpPercap", "pop"]].corr().round(2)
```

- Each pair of columns gets its r, and each column with itself gives 1
- `pop` and `lifeExp`: 0.05, almost no link between a country's size and its life
  expectancy

## Correlation Only Sees Straight Lines

```{python}
g2007["log_gdp"] = np.log(g2007["gdpPercap"])
print(round(g2007["log_gdp"].corr(g2007["lifeExp"]), 2))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 1.9))
axes[0].scatter(g2007["gdpPercap"], g2007["lifeExp"], s=12)
axes[0].set_xlabel("gdpPercap")
axes[1].scatter(g2007["log_gdp"], g2007["lifeExp"], s=12)
axes[1].set_xlabel("log_gdp")
axes[0].set_ylabel("lifeExp")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`np.log()` turns doublings into equal steps, as the log axis did in lecture 7. The curve
becomes a straight line, and r goes from 0.68 to 0.81.

## Correlation Is Not Causation

::: {.callout-important}
A correlation finds an **association**. Richer countries also have more doctors, cleaner
water and more schooling: income stands in for all of them.
:::

- You may write: *"in 2007, countries with higher incomes had longer life expectancies"*
- You may not write: *"raising income raises life expectancy"*
- r near 0 does not mean no relationship, only no **straight-line** one. Plot first, as
  Anscombe showed in lecture 7

# 2. Linear Regression Models in Python

## From Correlation to a Line

Correlation measures the link. **Linear regression** draws the line:

$$\text{lifeExp} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp} + e$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
fit_all = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g2007).fit()
xs = np.array([g2007["log_gdp"].min(), g2007["log_gdp"].max()])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.9))
ax.scatter(g2007["log_gdp"], g2007["lifeExp"], s=12)
ax.plot(xs, fit_all.params["Intercept"] + fit_all.params["log_gdp"] * xs, color="#C44E52")
ax.set(xlabel="log_gdp", ylabel="lifeExp")
plt.show()
```

- $b_0$, the **intercept**: the value of `lifeExp` when `log_gdp` is 0
- $b_1$, the **slope**: how much `lifeExp` changes when `log_gdp` increases by 1

## The Line of Best Fit

```{python}
#| echo: false
mini = g2007.sample(25, random_state=7)
fit_mini = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=mini).fit()
line_x = np.array([mini["log_gdp"].min(), mini["log_gdp"].max()])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.2))
ax.vlines(mini["log_gdp"], mini["lifeExp"], fit_mini.fittedvalues, color="#999999", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter(mini["log_gdp"], mini["lifeExp"], zorder=3)
ax.plot(line_x, fit_mini.params["Intercept"] + fit_mini.params["log_gdp"] * line_x,
        color="#C44E52")
ax.set(xlabel="log_gdp", ylabel="lifeExp")
ax.set_title("25 countries: each grey line is one residual", loc="left", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

- $e$, the **residual**: how far each country is from the line, actual minus predicted
- The **line of best fit** keeps the residuals as small as possible: its method is called
  **ordinary least squares**, or OLS

## Fitting a Model in Python

`smf.ols()` needs two things: a **formula**, the equation, and the **data**.

```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g2007).fit()
model.params.round(2)
```

- `smf.ols()` sets the model up, `.fit()` finds the line, and `.params` gives its two
  estimates: $b_0$, called `Intercept`, and $b_1$

## Reading the Estimates

The two estimates, back in the equation:

$$\text{lifeExp} = 4.95 + 7.20 \times \text{log_gdp}$$

- $b_1$ = **7.20**: one more unit of `log_gdp` is associated with **7.2 more years** of life
  expectancy
- $b_0$ = **4.95**: the prediction when `log_gdp` is 0, far outside the data. Do not
  interpret it
- Write *"is associated with"*, never *"causes"*

## From Equation to Formula

The formula is the equation, written for Python:

1. The `=` sign becomes `~`
2. Each predictor is added with `+`
3. No $b$ and no $e$: Python adds them itself

$$\text{lifeExp} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp} + e$$

```{.python}
smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g2007)
```

## More Than One Predictor

A categorical predictor, such as `continent`, goes inside `C()`:

$$\text{lifeExp} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp} + b_2 \times \text{continent} + e$$

```{.python}
smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp + C(continent)", data=g2007)
```

- Any number of predictors can be added the same way, each with `+`
- Section 3 reads what this model finds

## Your Turn: From Equation to Formula {background="#43464B"}

```{.python}
g1952["log_gdp"] = np.log(g1952["gdpPercap"])
model1 = smf.ols(____, data=g1952).fit()          # model 1, in quotes
model2 = smf.ols(____, data=g1952).fit()          # model 2, the continent inside C()
print(round(model1.params["log_gdp"], 2))
print(round(model2.params["log_gdp"], 2))
```

:::: {layout="[4,1]"}

[Model 1: $\text{lifeExp} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp} + e$]{style="font-size: 85%"}<br>
[Model 2: $\text{lifeExp} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp} + b_2 \times \text{continent} + e$]{style="font-size: 85%"}<br>

## Solution

```{python}
g1952 = gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 1952]
g1952["log_gdp"] = np.log(g1952["gdpPercap"])
model1 = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g1952).fit()
model2 = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp + C(continent)", data=g1952).fit()
print(round(model1.params["log_gdp"], 2))
print(round(model2.params["log_gdp"], 2))
```

With the continent in the model, the income slope falls from 8.83 to 4.77: part of what
income seemed to explain was the continent.

# 3. Linear Regression Results

## The Table of Estimates

`.summary()` prints the full results. Its second table, `.tables[1]`, holds the estimates:

```{python}
print(model.summary().tables[1])
```

- `coef`: the estimates, as in `model.params`
- The other columns say **how sure** we can be of each one

## How Sure Are We?

Other countries, or another year, would give a slightly different slope. The table says by
how much:

- `std err`, the **standard error**: how much the estimate would change with other data
- `[0.025  0.975]`, the **95% confidence interval**: slopes from 6.3 to 8.1 are compatible
  with the data
- `P>|t|`, the **p-value**: if the true slope were 0, how often would chance alone give one
  this far from 0? Below 0.05, the slope is **significantly** different from 0. Here,
  `0.000`
- A p-value is **not** the probability that the result is true
- A table showing `0.000` means below 0.0005: write **p < 0.001**

## How Well Does It Fit?

```{python}
print(round(model.rsquared, 2))
```

- **R² = 0.65**: the model accounts for 65% of the variation in life expectancy between
  countries
- The other 35% is how far countries sit above or below what their income predicts

::: {.callout-warning}
A high R² does not make a model right, nor a low one useless: judge it by what it is for.
:::

## A Categorical Predictor

```{python}
model2 = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp + C(continent)", data=g2007).fit()
print(model2.params.round(2))
```

- Africa, first in alphabetical order, is the **reference**: each continent's estimate is a
  difference from Africa
- **At the same income**, life expectancy is 11.3 years higher in Europe than in Africa, on
  average

```{.python}
g1952 = gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 1952]
```

:::: {layout="[3,2]"}

## Solution

```{python}
g1952 = gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 1952]
g1952["log_gdp"] = np.log(g1952["gdpPercap"])
model = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g1952).fit()
print(model.summary().tables[1])
print(round(model.params["log_gdp"], 2))
print(round(model.rsquared, 2))
```

Yes: p is below 0.001, and 0 is outside 7.52 to 10.14. Income accounted for 56% of the
variation in 1952, against 65% in 2007.

# 4. Prediction

## From Explaining to Predicting

- Sections 2 and 3 **explained**: how life expectancy goes with income, and how sure we
  are of it
- The same line can also **predict**: a best guess of a country's life expectancy, from its
  income alone
- Businesses predict all the time: tomorrow's sales, next month's demand, the price of a
  house

This section answers three questions, in order: how to predict, how wrong the predictions
are, and how to measure that honestly.

## Predicting One New Value

Back to the 2007 model. Fit it, put the new income in a table, and predict. Here, a country
with \$10,000 per person:

```{python}
model = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=g2007).fit()
new = pd.DataFrame({"log_gdp": [np.log(10000)]})
model.predict(new).round(1)
```

- `predict()` needs a table with the same column as the formula: `log_gdp`
- By hand: $b_0 + b_1 \times \text{log_gdp}$ = 4.95 + 7.20 × 9.21 = **71.3 years**
- A best guess, not a fact: real countries sit above or below the line

## Predicting for Several Countries

One row per country. `np.log()` takes the whole list of incomes at once:

```{python}
new = pd.DataFrame({"log_gdp": np.log([2000, 10000, 45000])})
model.predict(new).round(1)
```

- Rows 0, 1 and 2 are the incomes \$2,000, \$10,000 and \$45,000

::: {.callout-warning}
Only predict inside the range of the data: incomes from \$278 to \$49,357 in 2007. For
\$500,000, the line predicts 99.5 years. It has never seen such a country, and neither have
you.
:::

## How Wrong Are the Predictions?

To find out, predict the countries whose life expectancy we already know, and compare:

```{python}
g2007["predicted"] = model.predict(g2007)
g2007["error"] = g2007["lifeExp"] - g2007["predicted"]
g2007[["country", "lifeExp", "predicted", "error"]].round(1).head(4)
```

- The **error**: actual minus predicted, the residual of section 2
- Albania lives 8.9 years longer than its income predicts; Angola 23.3 years shorter

## One Number for All the Errors

```{python}
mae = g2007["error"].abs().mean()
rmse = np.sqrt((g2007["error"] ** 2).mean())
print("MAE", round(mae, 1), "years; RMSE", round(rmse, 1), "years")
```

- **MAE**, the mean absolute error: drop the signs with `.abs()`, then take the mean. A
  prediction misses by 5.1 years on average
- Why `.abs()`? Errors above and below the line would cancel out: their mean is 0
- **RMSE**, the root mean squared error: square the errors, take the mean, then the square
  root. Big misses count more
- Both are in **years**: the smaller, the better

## Marking Your Own Homework

The 5.1 years is too optimistic:

- These are the 142 countries that **drew the line**: OLS put it as close as possible to
  them
- A new country had no say in where the line goes, so it will usually be missed by more
- It is like practising on the exam paper itself: a great score, but it says nothing about
  a new paper

::: {.callout-important}
To know how wrong a model will be on **new** data, measure it on data it has **not** seen.
:::

## Train and Test

Before fitting, put a quarter of the countries aside:

```{python}
train = g2007.sample(frac=0.75, random_state=1118)
test = g2007.drop(train.index)
print(len(train), "countries to fit the model,", len(test), "to test it")
```

- **train**: 75% of the countries, drawn at random, to fit the model
- **test**: the other 25%, kept aside: for the model, they are new countries
- `random_state` fixes the random draw: the same split every time

Every machine learning model, from a regression to a neural network, is judged this way.

## Fit on Train, Measure on Test

```{python}
fit = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp", data=train).fit()
errors_train = train["lifeExp"] - fit.predict(train)
errors_test = test["lifeExp"] - fit.predict(test)
print("MAE on train:", round(errors_train.abs().mean(), 1), "years")
print("MAE on test:", round(errors_test.abs().mean(), 1), "years")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
xs = np.array([g2007["log_gdp"].min(), g2007["log_gdp"].max()])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.45))
ax.scatter(train["log_gdp"], train["lifeExp"], s=10, color="#23373b", label="train")
ax.vlines(test["log_gdp"], test["lifeExp"], fit.predict(test), color="#999999", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter(test["log_gdp"], test["lifeExp"], s=24, color="#EB811B", zorder=3, label="test")
ax.plot(xs, fit.params["Intercept"] + fit.params["log_gdp"] * xs, color="#C44E52")
ax.set(xlabel="log_gdp", ylabel="lifeExp")
ax.set_title("The line comes from train; each grey line is a test error", loc="left",
             fontsize=10)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

- Train: 4.9 years. Test: **5.7 years**, the honest figure for a new country
- The RMSE agrees: 6.7 years on train, 8.0 on test

## Why It Matters: Overfitting

```{python}
#| echo: false
tr = g2007.sample(12, random_state=7)
te = g2007.drop(tr.index)
grid = np.linspace(tr["log_gdp"].min(), tr["log_gdp"].max(), 300)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.3), sharey=True)
for ax, degree, name in zip(axes, [1, 8], ["Straight line", "Flexible curve"]):
    coef = np.polyfit(tr["log_gdp"], tr["lifeExp"], degree)
    mae_tr = (tr["lifeExp"] - np.polyval(coef, tr["log_gdp"])).abs().mean()
    mae_te = (te["lifeExp"] - np.polyval(coef, te["log_gdp"])).abs().mean()
    ax.scatter(te["log_gdp"], te["lifeExp"], s=10, color="#EB811B", alpha=0.5,
               label="test countries")
    ax.scatter(tr["log_gdp"], tr["lifeExp"], s=28, color="#23373b", label="12 train countries")
    ax.plot(grid, np.polyval(coef, grid), color="#C44E52")
    ax.set_ylim(30, 90)
    ax.set_xlabel("log_gdp")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: MAE {mae_tr:.1f} on train, {mae_te:.1f} on test", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A more flexible model can bend to pass close to every train country. Fitted on 12
countries, the curve misses them by 1.8 years on average, but misses the others by 12.9: it
has learned the **noise** of its 12 countries, not the pattern. This is **overfitting**,
and only the test set shows it.

## The Same Pattern in scikit-learn

**scikit-learn**, the main machine learning library, fits the same line on `train`:

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model_sk = LinearRegression()
model_sk.fit(train[["log_gdp"]], train["lifeExp"])
print(round(model_sk.intercept_, 2), model_sk.coef_.round(2))
print(fit.params.round(2).tolist())
```

- The same intercept and slope as `smf.ols()` on `train`
- Predictors in a table, hence two brackets; the outcome is one column
- Choose a model, `.fit()`, `.predict()`: the same three steps for every model

## What You Can and Cannot Write

> In 2007, across 142 countries, one more unit of log GDP per capita was associated with
> 7.2 more years of life expectancy (95% CI 6.3 to 8.1), and income accounted for 65% of
> the variation. On 36 test countries, kept aside from fitting, predictions missed by 5.7
> years on average.

- Numbers with their uncertainty and their scope
- No cause: "associated with", not "raises"
- No extrapolation: nothing about incomes outside \$278 to \$49,357

## Solution

```{python}
g2007["log_gdp"] = np.log(g2007["gdpPercap"])
train = g2007.sample(frac=0.75, random_state=1118)
test = g2007.drop(train.index)
fit2 = smf.ols("lifeExp ~ log_gdp + C(continent)", data=train).fit()
errors2 = test["lifeExp"] - fit2.predict(test)
print(round(errors2.abs().mean(), 1))
print(round(np.sqrt((errors2 ** 2).mean()), 1))
```

Yes: on the same 36 test countries, the average miss falls from 5.7 to 4.0 years, and the
RMSE from 8.0 to 6.0.
